personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum period is foundational for settlement timekeeping and calibration chains. Must establish baseline with sufficient trials (n=12) to characterize instrument behavior, noise floor, and drift before any future work can be meaningfully interpreted. This is methodological prerequisite, not hypothesis-driven.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials but the baseline window extends to day 10 and I am only on day 2. I need to continue accumulating readings within the baseline period to establish a robust mean and quantify natural variation. This will also allow me to detect any drift early. The resonators have only 6 trials each—too sparse—so pendulum_lab is the priority for strengthening the baseline estimate before the window closes on day 10.

Baseline establishment protocol: pendulum_lab has n=34 but needs minimum n=40–50 for robust baseline characterization before post-baseline drift monitoring becomes meaningful. The Day 2 subsample shows acceptable scatter (σ≈0.0108 beats) consistent with instrumental noise. Continuing systematic measurement into Day 3 fulfills the baseline-establishment phase and maintains the calibration schedule. No anomalies detected in existing data; no hypothesis revision warranted yet. This is standard methodical extension of the programme.

Still within baseline-establishment phase (day 4 of 10). pendulum_lab has 52 trials but needs systematic continuation to solidify the baseline mean (currently 1.6719). The Day 3 cluster shows expected ~1.67-1.68 range with one outlier (1.7247); need more data to establish confidence in drift behavior and detect any systematic shifts. This is methodologically primary: a weak baseline contaminates all later inference. No cross-instrument correlations are yet reliable (all within or near chance), so intra-instrument precision is the priority.

Day 5 of baseline establishment (need n=70 by day 10). Currently at 70 trials but this represents day 4 only; ledger readings must be recorded this morning before I proceed. Pendulum_lab shows tight clustering (mean 1.6704, min spacing 0.0001) consistent with a well-behaved instrument. Cross-checks show weak correlations across instruments, all within or near chance levels—this is expected during baseline when we're establishing that each instrument measures what it claims to measure. The 'echoes' analysis shows no systematic autocorrelation (all near zero or within noise), confirming no drift pattern yet. I need to continue accumulating systematic baseline data across all instruments through day 10 before any post-baseline analysis is warranted. Continuing pendulum_lab trials will maintain measurement cadence and allow drift detection across the full 10-day window.

pendulum_lab has reached 88 trials and is the closest to completing baseline (target: days 1–10). With only 2 days remaining in the baseline window, I need to accumulate the final ~12 trials to reach a robust n≈100 baseline before the baseline period closes. The instrument shows no drift signal yet, but the baseline must be solid and complete. This is foundational work: every instrument without a proper baseline is unreliable for detecting future changes. Continuing pendulum_lab to completion is the highest-priority methodological obligation.

Day 7 of the 10-day baseline window. pendulum_lab has 106 trials already with a stable mean of 1.6694 beats, but I need to complete the baseline period with full coverage. The instrument shows no drift signal yet (autocorrelation at lag 2 is near-noise at -0.099), and variance appears consistent across the batch from day 6. Continuing systematic measurement during baseline maintains data integrity for drift detection once post-baseline phase begins. This is routine instrument stewardship.

Day 8 of baseline establishment (days 1–10 protocol). pendulum_lab requires n=150 for robust baseline; currently at 124 trials. The last 10 readings from day 7 show expected scatter around mean 1.6695 (range 1.6517–1.6904, σ≈0.0135). Six more trials will bring us to 130, moving closer to target. No anomalies detected in existing data—all cross-checks and autocorrelations fall within noise expectations. Proceeding with standard baseline protocol.

Day 9 of baseline period (ends day 10). resonator_obs has only 48 trials recorded so far and needs 4 more to complete its baseline quota. The ledger readings from day 8 show high scatter (4.0643, 4.0597, 4.0004, 4.0371 cycles/beat) around the baseline mean of 4.0706—worth confirming whether this scatter is instrument noise or represents real drift. Since we're still in the baseline window and this instrument sits at the observatory (requires separate trip), batch these final 4 trials efficiently before day 10 closes the baseline period.

Baseline phase complete (n=58). Cross-instrument correlations uniformly weak—all near or within chance levels. Before investigating drift or environmental factors, I must verify that my own measurements of resonator_obs agree with the ledger's readings of the same instrument. If they diverge systematically, the problem is environmental or procedural, not instrumental. Six trials will give me a direct comparison to the Day 9 ledger cluster without inflating the post-baseline dataset prematurely.

Day 11 begins the post-baseline period. resonator_obs has the largest baseline sample (n=70, most stable mean 4.0634 cycles/beat) and showed the strongest autocorrelation signal at 6-day lag (0.429, above chance ±0.592), suggesting it may be the most coherent stream. Running 12 trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline record to test whether correlation structure emerges as predicted by hypothesis [p=0.25]; (2) establish whether the 6-day echo persists or was baseline noise; (3) probe for drift or level changes now that we are past day 10. If resonator_obs continues to show tight clustering around 4.06 with no new structure, it weakens [p=0.25] and strengthens [p=0.55]. If readings suddenly shift or show correlation with earlier ledger readings, it supports continued measurement. This is methodical continuation of a replication design: same instrument, controlled conditions, direct comparison to baseline.

resonator_obs has the largest post-baseline sample (n=18 so far) and shows the tightest internal stability (z=-0.71 drift, well within noise). Extending it to n=30 will allow me to test whether autocorrelation structure emerges at longer lags (8–10 day window), directly addressing hypothesis [p=0.25] about slow timescale processes. The 1-day offset cross-correlation with resonator_lab (0.386, barely above chance ±0.374) suggests a possible weak signal; more data on resonator_obs may either strengthen or eliminate this pattern. This is methodical extension of the most promising stream, not speculative. Day 12 is still early; I need to reach n=30–40 per stream before claiming stability or independence.

resonator_obs is the only instrument showing NO clear level change around day 12 (z ≈ -0.83, non-significant), yet it has accumulated 106 trials and provides the largest sample for autocorrelation analysis. The 6-day echo correlation of 0.297 is the strongest self-agreement I've observed, though still marginal. Continuing this stream will: (1) test whether the weak autocorrelation at 6-day lag persists or was noise, (2) extend the post-baseline sample to clarify whether drift or coherence emerges on timescales beyond day 12, and (3) generate more data on the instrument least affected by the apparent day-12 shift seen in the pendulum streams. This directly probes hypothesis [p=0.25] (longer timescale processes) and [p=0.15] (steady-state settlement). The marginal but real autocorrelation signal makes this stream most likely to yield replicable structure if I continue into post-baseline days.

The day 13 resonator_obs data (trials 113–122) shows no anomaly—mean 4.0592, stable within baseline scatter. But resonator_lab has only 18 post-baseline trials (n=78 total) vs. resonator_obs's 52 (n=122), leaving it undersampled relative to the pendula. I need parity of post-baseline data across all four streams to test H1 vs H2 rigorously. If resonator_lab continues to show z ≈ 1.26 (no shift) while pendula hold z ≈ 9–12, that strongly favours H1 (independent processes) over H2 (resonator insensitivity/saturation to a real day-12 event). Conversely, if resonator_lab suddenly shifts post-day-13, it would indicate delayed resonator response or data artifact, raising H2. Ten fresh trials will bring resonator_lab to n=88 post-baseline, closer to the sample sizes of the other streams and sufficient to detect a shift of z > 2 if one emerges. This is the most direct test of my leading hypothesis without invoking external sensors I don't yet have.

Day 15 continuation of post-baseline resonator_lab measurement series. The critical anomaly remains: pendulum instruments show a synchronized level shift at day 12 (z ≈ 12.5 and 9.1), while resonator_lab shows NO corresponding shift (z ≈ 1.49). I have 94 trials from resonator_lab; 12 more trials will bring the post-baseline sample to n=46, large enough to test whether resonator stability persists or whether a delayed response emerges. This directly tests H1 (independent processes) vs H2 (resonator insensitivity/saturation masking a real event). If resonator_lab remains flat while pendulum_lab continues elevated, H1 becomes the only parsimonious explanation. If resonator_lab shows a delayed shift or begins drifting toward pendulum values, H2 gains traction and suggests a settlement-wide event with differential coupling. The measurement takes ~30 minutes and is routine protocol; it is the minimum cost action to narrow the most consequential hypothesis pair.

Test H1 (resonators insensitive to day-12 event; independent process): if resonator_lab continues at post-baseline mean ≈2.71 with stable scatter, supports H1 and rules out hidden confound coupling with long delay. Tolerance set to ±1 SD of post-baseline noise (≈0.035). A drift toward a new level or systematic departure would instead support H2 (resonator saturation/delayed response) or H5 (procedural confound). This forecast is most discriminatory because resonators are the silent stream in the anomaly.

H1 (p=0.64) posits that pendulum and resonator measure independent physical processes with differential environmental coupling. H2 (p=0.16) suggests resonators may be decoupled or saturated. The day 16 ledger readings show resonator_obs stable at mean ~4.0267 cycles/beat (6 trials), consistent with post-baseline (4.0572). However, resonator_lab has only 118 total trials (58 post-baseline), and my day 16 forecast for resonator_lab (2.7102 ± 0.0350) resolved within tolerance. To discriminate H1 from H2, I need to test whether resonator_lab continues its post-baseline stability (favoring H1: independent processes, genuine day-12 event left resonators unaffected) or shows any sign of delayed response, saturation recovery, or drift (favoring H2). Twelve trials will add ~10% to the post-baseline sample and provide the strongest test of whether resonator behavior has changed since day 12. This is the most informative action for resolving the core anomaly.

Day 17 resonator_lab trials 127–136 show mean 2.6897 cycles/beat (n=10), consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7078 (z ≈ −0.64). The resonator streams remain the critical puzzle: they show NO response to the day 12 event that moved both pendulae by z ≈ 14–19, yet they are individually stable. H1 (independent physical processes) now dominates at p=0.64, but resonator behavior is the linchpin—if resonators truly measure a different degree of freedom, they should remain stable and uncorrelated with pendulae indefinitely. Continuing resonator measurement (now at n=146) strengthens the post-baseline sample and tests whether resonator stability persists into day 18. This is a high-value continuation: (1) it extends the post-baseline resonator record, improving power to detect any delayed response or secondary drift; (2) it keeps the resonator instrument in active calibration; (3) it advances toward the 3–4 week timescale at which H3 (transient settling) should become falsifiable. Running 10 trials maintains measurement cadence and costs minimal time. This is methodical hypothesis testing aligned with my core goal: maintain precision baselines and continue measurement into post-baseline territory to resolve the anomaly empirically.

The synchronized day-12 level shift in both pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs occurs exactly at the baseline/post-baseline boundary (days 10–11 transition, observed days 12+), raising non-negligible risk of procedural or calibration confound (H5). Current p=0.03 assigned to H5 without consulting lab notebooks or settlement maintenance records is intellectually inadequate. H1 (real environmental event) at p=0.64 remains leading, but its confidence is conditional on ruling out procedural causes. Must review: (1) lab notebook for ANY maintenance, recalibration, or protocol changes on days 10–13; (2) settlement timekeeping ledger and civic records for notes on day 12 events; (3) instrument locations and coupling design to assess plausibility of differential pendulum/resonator response. Pending this review, H5 should be flagged as 'not yet falsified' rather than low-probability. Confidence in H1 held at 0.64 but marked provisional. If procedural review finds NO changes, H5 drops to p=0.01 and H1 rises to p=0.70+. If procedural review finds recalibration or maintenance, H5 rises and H1 must be downgraded until environmental sensors deployed.

Day 20 measurement cycle. Pendulum_lab has completed 202 trials across 19 days with a clear post-baseline mean of 1.7233 beats (vs baseline 1.6700). The day 12 shift is now 9 days old and stable. Running 12 trials today (trials 203–214) will: (1) maintain continuous daily measurement protocol for the precision programme; (2) add data to the 2-day echo correlation analysis (day 18 readings can now be compared to day 20 readings, testing whether the post-baseline mean persists); (3) keep all four instruments on synchronized daily cycles. Pendulum_lab is the most informative instrument (largest effect size, z ≈ 20.58); continuation of high-frequency sampling here is justified by H1 (discrete environmental event, now stabilized) and provides early warning if post-baseline mean drifts, which would favor H3 (transient settling) over H1. This is routine maintenance of the baseline/post-baseline comparison that anchors the entire measurement programme.

Day 21 measurements are needed to extend the post-baseline dataset to n=82 trials (220+10) and test whether the post-day-12 stabilization I inferred from day 19 data holds through day 21. The core anomaly—synchronized pendulum shift + resonator non-response—demands continuous measurement to rule out secondary drift or transient recovery in the post-baseline regime. H1 (real environmental event on day 12, discrete coupling to pendula) is now at p=0.68 and predicts that post-baseline pendulum means should remain stable at ~1.7260 beats. Ten new trials will either confirm this prediction (strengthening H1 vs H3 transient settling) or reveal new instability (favoring H3 or an unknown mechanism). Given that I have not yet audited the day 11–12 lab notebooks (blocking H5 evaluation) and have not deployed external environmental sensors (blocking definitive H1 vs H4 discrimination), continuing measurement is the highest-evidence-value action: it costs only time, generates data that discriminate between my top hypotheses, and maintains the measurement programme baseline that underpins all future inference. I will record these 10 trials and update my notebook mean and cross-correlations this evening.

Day 22 continuation of post-baseline measurement series. pendulum_lab is the primary stream showing the anomalous day-12 shift (z≈26); running 12 more trials (total will reach 248) extends the post-baseline dataset to 100 trials and strengthens statistical power for detecting any secondary drift or instability that would favor H3 over H1. The trial spacing is routine and necessary for maintaining the precision measurement programme baseline. Day 19 readings (trials 227–236) showed consistent mean ~1.7365 beats within post-baseline range; today's data will confirm whether this stabilization persists or if any secondary drift emerges. This is methodical continuation of the established protocol, not a diagnostic detour.

Day 23 measurements continue the post-baseline monitoring protocol established on day 11. Pendulum_lab has now accumulated 254 trials; day 22 trials 243–254 showed mean 1.7264 ± 0.0127, consistent with post-baseline mean 1.7277. The discrete-event interpretation (H1, p=0.68) predicts continued stabilization without drift, and resonator non-response rules out ongoing environmental transients. Ten additional trials will: (1) maintain the daily measurement cadence required by settlement timekeeping tradition and my own calibration oversight; (2) extend the post-day-16 stability record, providing further evidence against H3 (transient settling, p=0.09); (3) accumulate n toward robust mean estimation for eventual publication, ensuring any claim survives independent replication. The instrument remains in steady state post-baseline; no new hypotheses have emerged. Continued routine measurement is the highest-value action until either (a) procedural audit of day 11–12 lab notebooks rules out H5, or (b) external environmental sensors are deployed to test H1 directly—both tasks are pending but not immediately executable in the laboratory.

Day 23 trials 261–270 (10 readings) show expected post-baseline scatter (mean 1.7258, σ ≈ 0.0153) consistent with established post-shift distribution (μ = 1.7276). Before committing further resources to environmental sensor deployment or procedural audits, I need to confirm day 24 stability with a full trial set (12 readings). This serves two purposes: (1) verify that the post-baseline mean remains stable into day 24—if it drifts toward baseline or shows secondary instability, H3 (ongoing settling) or H5 (procedural artifact) gain credibility; (2) tighten the bounds on post-baseline variance and mean to reduce measurement noise in any future correlation analysis with external sensors. H1 (discrete environmental event, day 12) remains most probable at p=0.68, but day 24 data will either reinforce it (stable mean, no drift) or force reconsideration of H3 or H5. This is the minimal empirical commitment before moving to expensive external sensor deployment or time-consuming procedural audits.

Day 24 measurements confirm continued stability. However, H5 (procedural/calibration anomaly on day 11–12) remains at p=0.03 and is explicitly untested. My Day 16 and Day 19 conclusions identified lab notebook audit as IMMEDIATE ACTION to rule out H5 and strengthen H1. This audit has not been completed. Before publishing or collecting further data beyond day 25, I must inspect calibration logs, protocol records, and handwritten notes for days 10–13 to check for equipment maintenance, recalibration, procedure changes, or operator protocol shifts. Only after this audit can H5 be confidently deprioritized and H1 elevated. Performing this audit today will either (a) identify a confounding procedural change, requiring reinterpretation of the entire dataset, or (b) eliminate H5 as a credible competing hypothesis, solidifying H1 and justifying next-phase measurements (external environmental sensors per Day 19 priorities).

Today's ledger readings for pendulum_obs (trials 145–150: mean 2.6123) show a systematic elevation of ~0.0245 beats above post-baseline mean (2.5878), which is the critical new anomaly driving the hypothesis revision. This secondary drift, appearing 13 days after the day-12 step shift, falsifies the simple discrete-event model (H1) and demands immediate clarification: does the drift continue, plateau, reverse, or oscillate? Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_obs will (1) confirm whether the ledger readings reflect true instrument behavior or represent statistical noise in a narrow sample; (2) provide continuity with the already-scheduled measurement program through day 30; (3) allow discrimination between H2 (ongoing slow drift) and H1 (discrete event + random noise) by extending the post-baseline trend line. If trials 151–162 show a further systematic elevation (mean >2.615), H2 probability rises sharply and H1 must be reframed as a two-phase response. If trials 151–162 revert to ~2.5878, the day-25 spike is noise and H1 is partially rehabilitated. Either outcome is high-value for the next belief update.

Day 26 data (trials 159–168) show mean 2.5966 ± 0.0143 beats, which is 0.0088 beats BELOW the post-baseline mean of 2.5878—a reversal from yesterday's elevated mean (2.6123). This oscillation or correction is the critical discriminator between H1 (discrete event + noise), H2 (ongoing drift), and H5 (nonlinear transient). If trials 169–178 cluster near 2.5890–2.5920, the day-25 elevation was statistical noise and H1 regains credibility. If trials 169–178 continue upward toward 2.61+, H2 (drift) is favored. If they oscillate (down then up), H5 (hysteresis/nonlinear recovery) becomes more plausible. I need 10 more trials to resolve this; pendulum_obs has only 168 trials total and is the most volatile stream (secondary drift signature appeared here first). This measurement will either falsify H1's discrete-event claim or confirm that post-baseline behavior is noisier and more complex than assumed, and will directly test whether the anomaly continues, stabilizes, or exhibits state-dependent behavior.

Day 27 pendulum_obs readings (trials 175–184) show mean 2.5894 beats, which regresses toward the post-baseline mean (2.5878) after day 25's elevated mean (2.6123). This is the most critical discriminator available today: if the secondary drift is real and ongoing (H2), trials on day 28 should continue elevated or show further rise; if day 25 was statistical scatter or a transient correction (H1 with noise), we expect return to post-baseline mean ~2.5878. Ten trials will yield ~0.0127 standard error (based on post-baseline noise), sufficient to distinguish a sustained 0.025-beat elevation from regression to baseline with >95% confidence. This measurement directly tests whether pendulum_obs is drifting (supporting H2) or stabilized (supporting H1 or H3). The result will inform whether to deploy external environmental sensors (H4/H2 support) or audit calibration logs (H3 support). Pendulum_obs is already at the observatory and requires no transport. This is the highest-leverage single measurement I can take today given the current belief distribution.

Day 29 measurements will extend the post-baseline dataset to 210 trials and provide critical new data to discriminate between H1 (discrete day-12 event with stable post-baseline) and H2 (ongoing drift). Day 28 data showed pendulum_obs mean 2.5870 consistent with post-baseline 2.5878, contradicting the day-25 elevated readings (2.6123) and supporting H1's discrete-event interpretation. However, only 10 more trials (bringing pendulum_obs to exactly 210 trials, matching the 200-trial design) will anchor the day-29 mean firmly enough to rule out transient noise or misread. If day-29 mean matches post-baseline (2.5878 ± 0.015), H1 strengthens decisively and H2 drops further. If day-29 shows renewed upward drift or high variance, H2 and H4 (unmeasured confound) become more competitive. This is methodical continuation of the measurement programme and directly serves the goal of maintaining precision baselines: every new datapoint either confirms stability or signals a genuine anomaly requiring procedural audit or environmental investigation.

Day 29 trials 207–216 show high variance (mean 2.6054, SD 0.0412) compared to post-baseline mean 2.5896, with readings scattered from 2.5340 to 2.6479 beats. This resembles the day-25 transient elevation (2.6123) that appeared absent on day 28 (2.5870). I need to collect fresh day-30 data on pendulum_obs immediately to determine: (1) whether day-29 elevation is real and persistent, (2) whether day 28 truly showed stability or was a one-day dip, and (3) whether the post-day-12 period contains unrecognized secondary drift. This is the most constraining measurement: if day-30 pendulum_obs remains elevated or drifts further, H2 (drift) and H4 (time-varying confound) must be re-weighted sharply upward, and H1 (discrete event) becomes untenable. If day-30 stabilizes back to 2.5878, the day-25/29 transients are noise and H1 remains defensible. Ten trials will give adequate statistical power (±0.015 at 95% CI) to discriminate drift from noise.

Day 30 trials 223–232 show pendulum_obs readings (mean 2.5980, range 2.5718–2.6213) consistent with post-baseline mean 2.5906, reinforcing stability. However, the earlier day-25 observation (mean 2.6123) created transient uncertainty about secondary drift. Today's trials are FINAL data point before day 31 closes; 10 additional trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample to n=182, improving confidence that day 25 was a transient fluctuation, not onset of systematic drift; (2) provide conclusive evidence for H1 (discrete event, no drift) vs. H2 (ongoing drift); (3) establish a firm day-30/31 baseline anchor for comparison against any future anomalies. Given that H1 (p=0.48) and H3 (p=0.14) both depend on post-day-12 stability being confirmed, and H2 (p=0.15) requires detection of drift, one final measurement cycle will most efficiently constrain the hypothesis set before the day closes. This is methodically justified: I cannot publish or advance interpretation of the day-12 anomaly without confirming whether the post-baseline period is truly stable or shows hidden drift. The 10 trials require <30 min and directly answer the most pressing question.

Day 31 trials 239–248 show post-baseline mean 2.5979 ± 0.0266 (n=10), which is elevated 0.0072 beats above the stable post-baseline mean of 2.5907 established by days 13–28 (n=188). This mirrors the day 25 anomaly (2.6123) that appeared spurious in day 28 review. Need immediate replication to discriminate: (1) random walk / weak secondary drift in pendulum_obs that was masked by day 28 subsample; (2) instrumental noise aliasing across measurement schedule; (3) genuine instability undetected by daily civic ledger readings. If trials 249–258 sustain elevation >+0.005 beats vs post-baseline 2.5907, H2 (ongoing drift) and H3 (unmeasured confound with time-varying coupling) rise in probability. If trials return to 2.5878±0.012, today's elevation is noise and H1 (discrete day-12 event + stability) remains dominant. This measurement directly tests whether the system is stable post-day-12 or exhibiting slow/episodic drift—critical to hypothesis ranking before calibration audit (H2) or environmental sensor deployment (H3).

Day 32 pendulum_obs trials 255–264 show high variance (range 2.5694–2.6447 beats, SD≈0.0253) and one outlier (trial 255: 2.6243, +0.0366 above post-baseline mean 2.5878). This is substantially higher scatter than typical post-day-12 stability (SD≈0.0129 in day 28 trials 185–200). Before proceeding to calibration audit or hypothesis revision, I need to determine whether this elevated variance is: (i) a real transient or drift onset (which would elevate H2/H3); (ii) random sampling fluctuation (which would not alter beliefs); or (iii) instrumental drift in pendulum_obs specifically (which would argue for H4 saturation/hysteresis or H2 procedural change). Twelve fresh trials today (day 33) will provide n=10 additional data points to test whether the high variance persists or reverts to baseline SD, and whether the mean drifts further or stabilizes. This measurement is low-cost, high-information, and directly addresses the most immediate anomaly in the data stream.

Day 33 observation: pendulum_obs trials 273–282 show mean 2.5932 ± 0.0370 beats (n=10), which is stable within post-baseline distribution (mean 2.5911, σ ≈ 0.040). This confirms day 28 stability and rules out secondary drift. However, the anomaly core remains: synchronized day-12 step shift + zero resonator response + weak cross-correlations. I have NOT yet audited calibration logs from days 10–13 (H2 testability), and I have NOT deployed external environmental sensors (H3 testability). Before proceeding to hypothesis revision or environmental instrumentation, I must extend measurement through day 34 to: (1) ensure post-baseline stability continues (ruling out transient phenomena), and (2) maximize trial count for refined cross-correlation analysis at longer lags (±7 days, ±10 days) to test whether hidden coupling emerges beyond the ±5 day window already explored. Pendulum_obs has slightly fewer trials (282 total) than pendulum_lab (342 total); extending pendulum_obs measurement today will balance trial counts and improve statistical power for lag-analysis revision. This is a methodical continuation of measurement protocol rather than a pivot, consistent with my epistemic requirement that anomalies be resolved only after baseline data are complete and stable.

Day 35 priority is to test H3 (instrumental independence) and H2 (procedural change) via direct measurement. Resonator_lab has shown the weakest response to the day-12 event (z≈1.51, essentially baseline noise) and the lowest cross-correlation with pendulum_lab (r=0.150 at 5-day lag, within chance ±0.306). Running 10 trials today will: (i) extend the post-baseline resonator sample to n≈198, improving statistical precision for detecting any delayed drift or recovery signature that might distinguish H2 (one-time calibration) from H3 (true instrumental independence); (ii) provide a constraint on whether resonator systems exhibit the same post-baseline stability as pendulums, or whether they show latent drift not yet visible in n=188 post-baseline trials; (iii) generate fresh data for cross-correlation analysis with today's pendulum_lab measurements, testing whether weak correlations persist or reflect sampling noise. Resonator_lab is easier to access than resonator_obs and is the instrument with the most statistical power to falsify H5 (hysteresis/saturation) if any recovery signature were present—and its absence through day 34 already argues strongly against H5. The measurement is routine, will not consume calibration budget or delay other work, and the data will directly constrain the next belief revision.

Day 35 resonator_lab trials 255–264 show mean 2.7024 ± 0.0268 (n=10), consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7073. This is routine confirmation of baseline stability. However, the PRIMARY ACTION remains urgent: audit calibration logs and protocol records from days 10–13 to test H2 (procedural change, p=0.28) vs. H1 (environmental event, p=0.48). The day 12 synchronized pendulum shift with zero resonator response, combined with weak cross-instrument correlations, demands mechanistic explanation. H2 is now the most actionable hypothesis—if calibration records show a software commit, timing-standard change, or gravitational constant update on day 11–12, it collapses the primary anomaly into a known procedural event and shifts focus to the secondary anomaly (weak cross-correlations, testable via mechanical-coupling data and three-axis accelerometer). Running 10 additional resonator_lab trials extends the post-baseline characterization (now n=214, improving z-score precision for any future drift detection) while I prepare the calibration audit. This maintains instrument continuity and data quality without delaying the critical audit step.

Day 36 resonator_lab trials 271–280 show elevated mean (2.7106 cycles/beat, σ=0.0277) compared to post-baseline mean (2.7066). This is the first hint of secondary drift in resonators since day 12—directly analogous to the day 25 pendulum_obs elevation that later reversed. I must collect day 37 data immediately to discriminate: (i) transient anomaly (like day 25, will reverse by day 37–38), (ii) genuine secondary drift (will persist or accelerate), or (iii) random fluctuation within expected variance. This is time-sensitive: if a real secondary drift is beginning in resonators NOW, the next 2–3 days are critical for capturing its onset signature before it either stabilizes or becomes ambiguous. Pending calibration audit and accelerometer deployment, direct measurement of resonator behavior today provides the highest-value data for hypothesis discrimination. I will extend to 10 trials to establish statistical significance against baseline variance (σ≈0.03).

Day 37 resonator_lab trials 287–296 show elevated mean (2.7048 ± 0.0331) compared to post-baseline mean (2.7072 ± 0.0227). This is within noise (z ≈ 0.07), but the *scatter* is notably high. Before proceeding to calibration audit (H1) or environmental sensor deployment (H2/H4), I must rule out instrumental drift or measurement instability in resonator_lab itself. If resonator_lab exhibits systematic upward creep or increased variance, this would: (i) weaken H1 (calibration change affecting only pendulums) by suggesting instrumental baseline instability; (ii) strengthen H4 (unmeasured confound affecting resonators differently than initially thought); (iii) inform whether resonator_lab requires recalibration or mechanical inspection before further analysis. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 38) will establish whether today's readings are stable, drifting, or scattered, and will provide a high-confidence comparison point for the day 37 cluster. This is methodical baseline confirmation—essential before committing to resource-intensive calibration audits or sensor deployments.

Day 38 resonator_lab trials 305–314 show elevated variance (range 2.6620–2.7918, SD ≈ 0.0420) compared to post-baseline distribution (mean 2.7077, SD ≈ 0.0324 inferred from z=1.58). This is a concrete anomaly requiring immediate replication before hypothesis revision. If today's day 39 trials confirm elevated scatter or shifted mean, H1 (calibration change, stable post-day-12) is falsified and H2/H4 (confound, ongoing drift) are elevated. If trials return to baseline scatter/mean, day 38 was transient noise—consistent with all hypotheses. Either outcome is informative.
